opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. I think the breakthrough with large language models is real, and it surprised almost everyone, including people like me who have been working in AI and robotics for decades. What's remarkable is that by training on an enormous corpus of text, essentially a big chunk of everything humans have written on the internet, these models learned to produce language that is fluent, coherent, and often genuinely useful. They can summarize, translate, write code, answer questions. That's something many of us didn't think would arrive this soon.

But I try to be careful about what exactly the breakthrough is. The key ingredient was data. There was this vast reservoir of text just sitting there, and with the transformer architecture and a lot of compute, it turned out you could extract an extraordinary amount of structure from it. In a sense, the models are compressing patterns in how humans use language, and because language encodes so much of what we know about the world, that compression captures a lot of apparent knowledge and reasoning.

Where I'd push back is on the leap people make from "it can talk about the world" to "it understands the world" or "we're about to have general intelligence that can do anything." Coming from robotics, I see a big gap. Language models are very good with symbols, but the physical world is a different matter. There's a phrase, Moravec's paradox, that captures it: the things that are hard for humans, like chess or calculus, turn out to be relatively easy for computers, and the things that are easy for a two-year-old, like picking up an unfamiliar object or folding a towel, are incredibly hard for machines.

And part of the reason is that there's no internet-scale dataset for robot manipulation. We have trillions of words of text, but we don't have anything close to that for the physics of grasping, the friction, the deformation of cloth, the uncertainty in sensing and control. I sometimes estimate the gap as something like a hundred thousand years of data, if you compare what's available for language to what's available for robot motion. So people expect that because ChatGPT arrived, a household robot that can clean up your kitchen is right around the corner. I think that's going to take longer than many people assume.

So my view is: it's a genuine and important breakthrough, it's going to change a lot of knowledge work, and it's also giving us useful tools for robotics, like better high-level planning and the ability to interpret instructions. But it's not magic, and we should be humble about how far it transfers to embodied intelligence in the physical world.

r002.rationale: The response says the breakthrough surprised almost everyone and that a vast reservoir of internet text, combined with transformers and compute, yielded extraordinary structure and strong performance.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I'll be honest, I was surprised. I've been working in AI and robotics for over thirty years, and like a lot of people in the field, I had come to expect incremental progress. So when ChatGPT came out, I was genuinely stunned. I think most of my colleagues were too. Nobody I know predicted that scaling up a next-word predictor on internet text would produce something that could write coherent essays, pass the bar exam, and carry on a conversation that feels remarkably fluent.

The way I understand it, the breakthrough is really about language. Language is something humans have been accumulating and refining for thousands of years. It's this enormous, structured record of how we think and how we describe the world. And it turns out that if you train a big enough model on enough of it, the statistical structure of that text captures an astonishing amount of what we'd call knowledge, reasoning, even a kind of common sense. The key ingredients were the transformer architecture, massive amounts of data, and massive compute, and the surprise was that it kept getting better the more you scaled it. That's not something we'd seen before in quite this way.

But I think it's important to be precise about what the breakthrough is and what it isn't. These models are extraordinary at manipulating symbols and text. What they don't have, at least not yet, is a body. They haven't learned from physical interaction with the world. And that matters a lot for my field, because robotics is fundamentally about the physical world, about perception and manipulation and dealing with uncertainty in real time.

There's an old idea called Moravec's paradox, which says that the things that are hard for humans, like playing chess or doing calculus, turn out to be relatively easy for computers, and the things that are easy for humans, like picking up a cup or folding laundry, turn out to be incredibly hard for robots. Large language models are, in a way, the ultimate confirmation of that. They can write poetry, but they can't clear a dinner table. A six-year-old can do things with their hands that no robot in the world can do today.

So I see the breakthrough as real and profound, but also as narrower than the hype suggests. There's been a tendency to say, well, language is solved, so robotics is next, and it'll fall in a couple of years. I'm skeptical of that. One reason is data. Language models had the entire internet to learn from. There's no equivalent corpus for physical manipulation. We don't have a trillion examples of robots grasping objects, and collecting that data is slow and expensive because it has to happen in the real world, one trial at a time. I've called this the hundred-thousand-year data gap, because that's roughly how long it would take to collect an internet's worth of robot experience at current rates. Now, that's a bit of a provocation, but the point stands.

That said, I think the language models are already useful to robotics in indirect ways. They can help with high-level planning, with interpreting instructions, with giving a robot some common-sense knowledge about what objects are and what they're for. And the vision-language models are starting to help with perception. So it's a wonderful tool. It's just not the whole answer. The hard part, the part I've spent my career on, is still the physics, the contact, the uncertainty. And I think that's going to take longer than people expect, and it's going to require good old-fashioned engineering alongside the learning.

r001.rationale: The response says training text captures statistical structure and that models manipulate symbols, but does not explain their novel outputs as recombinations of patterns from training data.

r002.rationale: The response says people were surprised that scaling a next-word predictor trained on internet text produced fluent, capable performance, and describes the internet as the data source behind that result.

astra-6.text:
I think one way to understand it is that language has more structure than we appreciated. We’ve known for a long time that words aren’t independent: If I give you the beginning of a sentence, you can often guess what comes next. What’s surprising is how far you can get by learning those relationships at an enormous scale. You start with predicting the next token, and you end up with a system that can translate, write code, and produce explanations that look remarkably sophisticated.

As a roboticist, I find that both exciting and humbling. In robotics, we’ve spent decades trying to build explicit models of the world. Here’s an approach that learns from examples and captures something that we haven’t been able to specify by hand.

But I would distinguish that breakthrough from having a system that can reliably act in the physical world. Language gives you an extraordinary amount of information, but it doesn’t give you everything. If a robot is picking up a glass, the friction, the weight, and the exact point of contact matter. And when it gets something wrong, it can’t simply generate another sentence.

So I see language models as a major breakthrough, and as a powerful ingredient for robotics. The interesting question is how to connect that broad knowledge to perception and action, while giving the system a good sense of when it’s uncertain.

r001.rationale: The response says models learn relationships from examples at enormous scale, but does not explain their novel outputs as recombinations of patterns encountered in training data.

r002.rationale: It mentions enormous-scale learning, but does not identify internet data as sufficient for the observed performance.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the breakthrough is that we’ve discovered how much structure there is in language, and how much of that structure a system can learn simply by trying to predict what comes next. That sounds like a very narrow task. But to do it well, you have to capture relationships between concepts, facts about the world, and something that looks remarkably like reasoning.

What’s especially striking to me, coming from robotics, is the contrast with physical action. We have these systems that can write a sonnet or explain a mathematical idea, and yet getting a robot to reliably pick up an unfamiliar object is still difficult. Language gives us this enormous resource of examples that people have already produced. In robotics, we don’t have anything comparable at that scale.

So I see it as a tremendous breakthrough, but I’m cautious about extrapolating from fluency in language to competence in everything else. The exciting question is how we connect these capabilities to perception and action, and how we establish when we should trust the result.
